prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
The alarm is still silent. Then, suddenly, your eyes open.

You look at the clock, and it is almost the time you planned to get up. It can feel as if your body knew what the clock was about to say.

Researchers think several body processes may be involved.

First, we have a body clock. Light is its strongest outside signal. Regular times for sleeping and waking can also help set this clock.

In one lab study, healthy adults were kept away from normal clocks and daylight. Very weak light and a regular sleep-and-wake schedule usually helped their body clocks match a 24-hour day. But the same setup usually did not match a day of 23.5 hours or 24.6 hours. This suggests that the body clock can follow a daily schedule, but it is not a perfect timer for every minute.

The end of the night may also make waking easier. Deep sleep usually becomes less common as the night continues. Lighter sleep and dream sleep become more common. Still, this alone cannot explain why someone wakes just before a certain alarm time.

Another part may be preparation. In one experiment, people were told when their sleep would end. A body signal called ACTH rose about one hour before waking. Researchers said this rise may show not only the daily body rhythm, but also preparation for the expected end of sleep.

Researchers also study “self-awakening.” This means waking near a planned time without an outside signal. A review found 17 studies with 715 people, but the methods were not all the same. In one small study, 7 of 15 people woke within 30 minutes of their planned time. In another study, 11 students tried this for a week. By the seventh day, their success rate was 82 percent.

Other small studies found changes before waking. Activity in the front part of the brain changed about 30 minutes before waking in successful participants. During a short nap, heart rate began to rise about three minutes before waking.

These findings suggest that the body may begin preparing before an expected wake-up time. But most studies asked people to think about a target time and try to wake then. They did not directly test people who happened to wake just before a real alarm. So, science cannot yet say that the body predicts an alarm time exactly.

【Point One】
Opening your eyes before the alarm does not mean your brain is fully ready for work. Research links abrupt waking from deep N3 sleep with stronger sleep inertia than waking from lighter N2 sleep, while REM falls between them. A nap study also found related brain-function differences after waking from N3.

【Point Two】
In a home study of 201 adults, free cortisol began rising, on average, about three hours before waking and peaked about half an hour afterward. Its rise did not speed up sharply at the waking boundary. A separate study of 16 men found a marked rise in ACTH and cortisol after waking, suggesting preparation unfolds across phases, not as a minute-perfect countdown.

point_one.reasoning: 睡眠慣性という、目覚めた直後の働きにくさを導入し、N3・N2・REMで影響が異なることを示している。Full Storyにはない具体的な実用的含意があり、単なる睡眠段階の要約ではない。

point_two.reasoning: 201人の研究によるコルチゾールの上昇時期や、16人の研究でACTH・コルチゾールが起床後にも上昇するという時間的な詳細を加えている。これは、起床準備がアラーム時刻に向けた一瞬の予測ではなく複数段階で進むことを具体的に示し、Full Storyの説明を実質的に深めている。
